title: Rome crosses to Sicily
summary: The Mamertines, ex-mercenaries holding Messana, ask both Carthage and Rome for help. Rome sends consul Appius Claudius Caudex across the strait: the first Roman army ever to fight outside Italy.
significance: A squabble over one city turned into a 23-year war for Sicily between the two strongest states in the west.
questions: Why did Rome risk war over Messana?

title: Agrigentum falls
summary: After a siege of about seven months, Rome takes Carthage's main base in central Sicily. Polybius says 25,000 of its people were sold into slavery.
significance: Rome now aimed to drive Carthage out of Sicily altogether, and realised it could not do that without a fleet.

title: Battle of Mylae: Rome's first sea victory
summary: Rome builds a fleet from scratch, reportedly copying a wrecked Carthaginian warship. Consul Gaius Duilius fits his ships with the corvus, a spiked boarding bridge that turns sea fights into infantry fights, and beats the Carthaginian navy.
significance: Rome's soldiers could now fight at sea. Duilius was honoured with a column decorated with the rams of captured ships.

title: Battle of Cape Ecnomus
summary: A Roman fleet carrying an invasion army to Africa smashes through the Carthaginian navy off southern Sicily. By Polybius' numbers it may be the largest sea battle ever fought.
significance: The road to Africa lay open. Consul Marcus Atilius Regulus landed and marched on Carthage.

title: Regulus crushed near Tunis
summary: Carthage hires a Spartan mercenary, Xanthippus, who fights on open ground with elephants and cavalry. Regulus' army is destroyed and he is captured. Then a storm wrecks most of the Roman fleet sent to evacuate the survivors.
significance: Rome's first invasion of Africa ended in disaster. Roman legend later made Regulus a hero who chose torture over betraying Rome, a story most historians doubt.

title: Battle of Drepana
summary: Consul Publius Claudius Pulcher attacks the Carthaginian fleet in harbour. When the sacred chickens refuse to eat, a bad omen, he throws them overboard: 'Let them drink, then.' He loses most of his fleet.
significance: Rome's worst naval defeat of the war. Claudius was put on trial back home.

title: Hamilcar Barca takes command
summary: Hamilcar Barca seizes a mountain stronghold behind Roman lines and raids the coast of Italy for years. Around this time his son Hannibal is born.
significance: Hamilcar was never beaten in Sicily. He came home convinced Carthage had given up too easily.

title: Battle of the Aegates Islands
summary: With the state broke, wealthy Romans fund a new fleet with private loans. It catches a slow, heavily laden Carthaginian supply fleet and destroys it. Carthage asks for peace.
significance: Carthage leaves Sicily and pays 3,200 talents over ten years. Sicily becomes Rome's first overseas province.

title: The Mercenary War
summary: Carthage's unpaid mercenaries, back from Sicily, revolt and are joined by its Libyan subjects. The war is notoriously savage. Hamilcar finally crushes the rebels in a gorge known as the Saw.
significance: Carthage survived, but the crisis gave Rome its chance to grab Sardinia.

title: Rome seizes Sardinia
summary: While Carthage is weak, Rome takes Sardinia and threatens war unless Carthage hands it over and pays another 1,200 talents. Carthage has no choice.
significance: Even Polybius, an admirer of Rome, called it unjust. He saw Carthaginian anger over Sardinia as a root cause of the next war.

title: Hamilcar goes to Spain; Hannibal's oath
summary: Hamilcar leaves to build a new Carthaginian empire in Spain, rich in silver and soldiers. Before he goes, his nine-year-old son Hannibal swears at an altar never to be a friend of Rome.
significance: The oath story comes from Hannibal himself, as told to a Syrian king decades later. Spain became the Barca family's power base.

title: New Carthage founded
summary: Hamilcar drowns in 228 BC. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair takes over and founds a new capital on a superb harbour, close to rich silver mines.
significance: Spanish silver paid for the army that Hannibal would take over the Alps.

title: The Ebro Treaty
summary: Rome, worried about a Gallic invasion of Italy, agrees with Hasdrubal that Carthage will not cross the Ebro in arms.
significance: It left the town of Saguntum, south of the Ebro but friendly with Rome, in an ambiguous position. That ambiguity started the next war.

title: Hannibal takes Saguntum
summary: Hannibal, commander in Spain since 221 BC, besieges Rome's friend Saguntum for eight months and takes it. Roman envoys go to Carthage. One holds up a fold of his toga: in it, he says, are peace and war. The Carthaginians tell him to choose. He chooses war.
significance: The Second Punic War begins, and Hannibal has already planned to fight it in Italy.

title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
stat: Arrived with about 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry (Polybius)
summary: Hannibal marches from Spain through southern Gaul, crosses the Rhône and climbs the Alps as winter sets in, harassed by mountain tribes. The crossing takes fifteen days and costs him a large part of his army.
significance: Rome expected to fight in Spain and Africa. Instead the enemy was in northern Italy, where the Gauls were ready to join him.

title: Battle of the Trebia
summary: Hannibal provokes consul Sempronius into wading the freezing river at dawn on an empty stomach. His brother Mago, hidden in a gully, hits the Romans from behind. Only about 10,000 Romans cut their way out.
significance: Hannibal's first great victory in Italy. Thousands of Gauls joined him.

title: Ambush at Lake Trasimene
summary: Consul Flaminius chases Hannibal along the lake shore into a morning fog. Hannibal's army is waiting on the hills above. The Roman column is trapped against the water and destroyed, and Flaminius is killed.
significance: Rome appointed a dictator, Fabius Maximus, who refused to fight Hannibal head-on. It earned him the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer.

title: Battle of Cannae
summary: Rome fields the biggest army in its history, about 86,000 men, to crush Hannibal once and for all. Hannibal lets his centre bend back, then closes his flanks and cavalry around the Roman army. It is surrounded and almost wiped out. Consul Aemilius Paullus dies on the field.
significance: The worst day in Roman history and the most famous double envelopment ever fought, still studied by armies today. Yet Rome refused to negotiate, and much of southern Italy went over to Hannibal.
questions: Why didn't Hannibal march on Rome after Cannae?
How did the double envelopment work?

title: Syracuse falls; Archimedes killed
summary: Syracuse switched to Carthage's side in 214 BC. Marcellus besieges it for two years, held off by Archimedes' war machines: catapults and cranes that lifted ships from the water. When the city falls, a Roman soldier kills Archimedes.
significance: Sicily was secured for Rome, and Syracuse's art treasures were shipped to Rome, giving Romans a taste for Greek art.

title: Hannibal at the gates
summary: To draw Roman armies away from besieged Capua, his biggest ally, Hannibal marches to within a few miles of Rome. Rome holds its nerve. Livy says the field where Hannibal camped was sold in Rome at full price that very week. Capua falls and is brutally punished.
significance: 'Hannibal ad portas' became a Roman bogeyman phrase for generations. The tide in Italy was turning.

title: The Scipio brothers killed in Spain
summary: Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, who had kept the Carthaginians busy in Spain for seven years, split their forces. Abandoned by their Spanish allies, both are killed in separate defeats.
significance: Rome sent Publius' 25-year-old son to take over. He would become Scipio Africanus.

title: Scipio storms New Carthage
summary: Young Scipio marches on Carthage's Spanish capital and takes it in a day, sending troops to wade across the lagoon at low tide while the defenders face the main assault.
significance: Carthage lost its main base, its silver, and the Spanish hostages it kept there.

title: Battle of the Metaurus
summary: Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crosses the Alps with a second army. Consul Claudius Nero secretly marches north to join his colleague, and together they destroy it. Hasdrubal is killed, and his head is thrown into Hannibal's camp.
significance: Hannibal's last real hope of reinforcement was gone.

title: Battle of Ilipa
summary: Scipio fakes his usual deployment for days, then switches it on the morning of battle and outflanks the Carthaginians on both wings.
significance: Carthaginian power in Spain was finished. Scipio had learned Hannibal's lessons.

title: Scipio invades Africa
summary: Against the advice of the cautious Fabius, Scipio lands in Africa. He burns the enemy camps in a night attack and wins the Numidian prince Masinissa to Rome's side.
significance: Carthage was under direct threat and called Hannibal home.

title: Hannibal leaves Italy
summary: After fifteen years in Italy, never beaten in a major battle there, Hannibal sails home from Croton to defend Carthage.
significance: He had won the battles and lost the war of endurance. Rome's alliance network in central Italy never broke.

title: Battle of Zama
summary: Hannibal opens with 80 elephants. Scipio's men leave lanes in their lines and the elephants run through them or turn on their own side. The Roman and Numidian cavalry chase off Hannibal's horse, then return to strike his infantry from behind.
significance: Hannibal's decisive defeat. Scipio took the name Africanus.

title: Carthage accepts Rome's terms
summary: Carthage gives up Spain and all but ten warships, pays 10,000 talents over 50 years, and agrees not to make war without Rome's permission. Masinissa becomes king of a united Numidia.
significance: Carthage was now a client state. The war-permission clause would be its undoing.

title: Hannibal flees into exile
summary: Elected chief magistrate of Carthage, Hannibal cleans up the state finances and makes enemies. When Rome demands his surrender, he escapes east to the Seleucid king Antiochus III.
significance: Rome's greatest enemy was now advising its next one.

title: Death of Hannibal
summary: Hunted from court to court, Hannibal is about to be handed over to the Romans. He takes poison, aged about 64.
significance: Scipio Africanus died around the same time, in self-imposed exile from Roman politics.

title: 'Carthage must be destroyed'
summary: After visiting a booming Carthage, the elderly senator Cato ends every speech, on any subject, with the call that Carthage must be destroyed. Plutarch says he dropped fresh figs from Carthage on the Senate floor to show how close the enemy was.
significance: Carthage had paid off its indemnity and was rich again. Fear and greed in Rome did the rest.

title: The Third Punic War begins
summary: Carthage fights back against Numidian raids without Rome's permission. Rome lands an army, and Carthage surrenders hostages and its weapons. Then Rome demands the people abandon their city and resettle about ten miles inland. They refuse, and fight.
significance: With no weapons left, Carthaginians made new ones day and night; Appian says women cut their hair for catapult ropes.

title: Carthage destroyed
summary: Scipio Aemilianus breaks into the city. After six days of street fighting the citadel surrenders. About 50,000 survivors are sold into slavery and the city is razed. Watching it burn, Scipio is said to have wept and wondered if Rome would one day share its fate.
significance: Its land became the Roman province of Africa. The story that Rome sowed the ground with salt is a modern invention.
